title: The Skinny on Probiotics
summary: Josh and Chuck explain probiotics: live bacteria believed to benefit gut health, their history from Elie Metchnikoff's work on Bulgarian peasants and sour milk and Henri Tissier's study of breastfed infants' bifidobacteria, the WHO definition, and functional foods like Activia. They cover the Danone settlement with the FTC and state attorneys general over overstated claims, what the science does and doesn't support (diarrhea, IBS, antibiotic-related diarrhea, Crohn's still unclear), the CFU dosing recommendation of at least one billion, prebiotics and symbiotics, freeze-drying and viability problems, supplement quality concerns, safety warnings (pancreatitis, compromised immune systems), and emerging research on the gut-brain connection. The episode closes with a listener mail from an archaeologist.

segments.summary: Hosts chat about a prank, the new Studio Show Notes video series on YouTube, and tease the probiotics topic, including Chuck's stomach trouble after a Guatemala trip.

segments.title: History of probiotics
segments.summary: Definition of probiotics and the history: Elie Metchnikoff's study of Bulgarian peasants and sour milk with lactobacillus, and Henri Tissier's study of bifidobacterium in breastfed infants, which challenged germ theory.

segments.title: Functional foods and Activia settlement
segments.summary: Probiotics added to food create functional foods that the FDA does not regulate. Danone's Activia claims about regularity and cold and flu were challenged by the FTC and state attorneys general, leading to a settlement of about $21 million and more general claims.

segments.title: Why people want probiotics and the state of the science
segments.summary: The appeal of probiotics for gut health, and a review of what the evidence supports: reducing diarrhea, IBS, and antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Crohn's disease and other claims remain unproven, with studies just beginning.

segments.title: Dosage, CFUs and strain specificity
segments.summary: Colony forming units, the 2013 expert panel recommending at least one billion CFUs, the problem that genus-level claims are too broad, and the Human Microbiome Project's role in identifying healthy gut profiles. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium affect immune proteins such as immunoglobulin A and beta defensins.

segments.title: Prebiotics, symbiotics and product viability
segments.summary: Prebiotics are food for probiotics, often dietary fiber; symbiotics combine both, as in yogurt, kefir, and kimchi. Freeze-drying protects shelf-stable products, while refrigerated products are more fragile. Many bacteria may die before reaching the gut.

segments.title: Supplement quality and safety
segments.summary: Consumer Lab findings that some probiotics lacked the advertised bacteria count. Probiotics are generally considered safe for healthy people, but a pancreatitis study showed more deaths in the probiotic group, and people with compromised immune systems should be cautious.

segments.title: Gut-brain connection and future research
segments.summary: Canadian research linking probiotics to lower anxiety and stress, a British Journal of Nutrition study of weight loss in women, the serotonin gut-brain link, and rodent studies on high-fat diets. Hosts suggest following up later.

segments.title: Practical advice
segments.summary: Advice for listeners: try probiotics since they are unlikely to hurt, check peer-reviewed research for specific conditions, and consider NIH guidance, while being wary of cheap grocery store products.

segments.title: Listener mail from an archaeologist
segments.summary: A listener who is an archaeologist praises the show's accuracy on archaeology, critiques the grid-square excavation example and the mention of brushes, and mentions Stalingrad SS archaeologists. Sign-off with contact info.
